author: Aizel Tugalon
title: Progressive solons file bill, resolutions on academic freedom
content:
Photo by John Andrei Rarang, The Staple

Progressive lawmakers under the Makabayan bloc filed House Bill No. 11678, or the Academic Freedom Act on Monday, October 12, a bill seeking to defend academic freedom.

The bill came after recent attacks on academic freedom, such as the suspension of four University of Santo Tomas (UST) student activists for protesting against a campus exhibit by the Philippine Air Force (PAF) and the red-tagging of students and faculty members of the University of the Philippines Rural High School (UPRHS).

In her statement, Kabataan Partylist Rep. Renee Co condemned attempts to silence students who have been at the forefront of the fight for social justice and against corruption, especially since the onset of the flood control scandal.

“Discipline offices and military propaganda must not be used to silence students who are simply asking questions about and wanting to stop state abuse,” the statement read.

The bill, which adopts the 2024 UN Draft Principles for Implementing the Right to Academic Freedom and the 2026 Special Rapporteur Report on Youth Activism, seeks to impose imprisonment and fines on violations of academic freedom, such as militarization of campuses, infiltrating student organizations, filing disciplinary punishments against students who engage in peaceful political dissent, and enacting threats and violence against members of the a

author: Aizel Tugalon
title: 17 Filipino workers in British Columbia fight back against labor trafficking
content:
TORONTO – Seventeen Filipino temporary foreign workers (TFW) in British Columbia (B.C) have come forward to campaign against fraudulent recruitment agency Helping Hands Immigration Services (HHIS) that trafficked them into precarious conditions.

In a press conference held with Migrante BC and Damayan BC, the workers described how they became victims of labor trafficking, including being forced to work long hours, receiving inadequate pay, and experiencing wage theft.

The 17 migrant workers who came from Taiwan, worked over four months in Newfoundland as seasonal workers at a seafood processing plant. After their seasonal employment, they were referred to HHIS recruiters Cherry May Ricafort and Vincent Macalipay to process extension of work permits. According to the workers, the two allegedly took advantage of the situation knowing that they were newcomers and that their work statuses were about to expire.

“We left the Philippines with our hopes and dreams. With the desire for a better future for our families, we took risks working in different countries,” one of the workers said.

In the Canadian immigration system, the Temporary Foreign Worker Program allows Canadian employers to hire foreign workers to fill temporary jobs when qualified Canadians are not available.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Victims’ families hope document dispute won’t delay ICC trial
content:
Victims’ families are hopeful that the trial will continue as the fourth status conference of Rodrigo Duterte’s alleged crimes against humanity before the International Criminal Court (ICC) concluded on October 13.

“This is important for us, because we are closely watching for justice to prevail through the ICC,” Dahlia Cuartero, mother of victim Jesus Cuartero, told the media in Filipino. “Justice here in the Philippines is hopeless.”

Duterte attended the status conference for the second time. The ICC Trial Chamber III discussed the preparations, including matters involving witnesses, evidence, disclosures, and the schedule of the first week of trial.

Similar to the previous status conference, ICC Presiding Judge Joanna Korner asked the prosecution to review the relevance of documents to avoid duplication.

The ICC Senior Trial Lawyer Julian Nicholls said that they have a team of analysts and experts that reviewed each document presented for trial.

The prosecution will also use government data like Philippine National Police (PNP) records and the accomplishment report of the Presidential Communications Operations Office (PCOO) to present the number of killings during Duterte’s presidential term.

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: ‘Dropping 3 impeachment articles vs Duterte compromises accountability’
content:
Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

The Senate impeachment court granted the prosecution’s manifestation to drop three articles of impeachment against Vice President Sara Duterte as it wanted to focus “on what is necessary.” For progressive groups, however, this move undermines calls for accountability.

“Ultimately, the prosecution chose political convenience over true accountability,” said human rights lawyer and former Bayan Muna Party-list Rep. Carlos Isagani Zarate in a statement.

After its earlier manifestation to drop Article III, which accused Sara of bribery, on October 13, the prosecution decided to also drop Article I (alleged misuse of confidential funds) and Article IV (assassination threats). Lead prosecutor Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro told the impeachment court that they would only focus on Article II which accuses the Vice President of having alleged unexplained wealth, false statements of assets, liabilities, and net worth (SALNs), and prohibited business interests.

Luistro said that the prosecution has presented sufficient evidence on Article II “to stand on its own.”

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison, on the other hand, acknowledged the prosecution’s power to withdraw its allegations but she said that the prerogative should not affect how they would counter the accusations against Duterte.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Workers win illegal dismissal case vs Lazada, manpower agencies
content:
In two separate cases, the National Labor Relations Commission (NLRC) has ruled in favor of platform workers in illegal dismissal cases against manpower companies and leading Southeast Asian e-commerce platform Lazada.

Both cases involve illegal dismissal and non-payment of the 13th month pay.

Josiah David Quising, legal representative of the platform workers in two separate cases, declared that “these victories are important because of the evolving nature of the workplace.”

“We are no longer traditional wherein workers are situated in one physical space, it also extends to the digital space,” Quising told Bulatlat in Filipino.

NLRC is an attached quasi-judicial agency of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) mandated to resolve labor and management disputes involving Filipino workers.

“These winning cases are mere reaffirmation of the rights of platform workers, particularly riders, based on the Supreme Court (decision),” Quising added.

The first case was an illegal dismissal with claims for non-payment of the 13th month pay, cash bond deposit, damages and attorney’s fees by a platform rider against Metro Courier Inc. (MCI) and Lazada.

The NLRC stated that the rider is a “regular employee of respondent Lazada and that he was illegally dismissed by the latter.”

The rider was employed by the manpower services MCI for Lazada. His regular work routine was described

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Six years on, a mother grieves death of son killed in the ‘drug war’
content:
Lorna Carina Pepaño. Screengrab from the Philippine Truth Commission

“For me, justice and healing mean holding accountable those who carried out the killings, the perpetrators, those who gave the orders, and the highest-ranking officials behind the killings.”

Trigger warning: details of violence and death

Seeing her son’s body, his blood spilling in the streets, Lorna Carina Pepaño could not cry. That day, on May 18, 2020, her son Christian was shot dead by two unidentified men while buying medicines and coffee for Pepaño.

On the day of the incident, Pepaño ran to the scene of the crime without slippers. Many of the witnesses she talked to said that Christian was begging for his life, telling the perpetrators that he was not the person they were after. The witnesses also heard one of the gunmen saying that Christian was not the target.

Six years later, Pepaño mustered the courage to tell the story of her son during the fourth public truth-telling session organized by the independent Philippine Truth Commission on October 9, 2026.

“All I feel until now is anger,” Pepaño said in Filipino. “Back then, I was shouting, saying words I never thought I could say. Never did I think that my son would be killed that day. I have so many questions but not a single answer.”

author: Alyssa Mae Clarin
title: US-based Filipino migrants protest prolonged ICE detention of slain journalists’ son
content:
Supporters of Mark Mabasa from the Tanggol Migrante Movement and other groups stage a protest in front of Adelanto City Hall after Mabasa's hearing was postponed. Photo by BAYAN USA

Mabasa’s detention is part of a broader pattern of attacks against migrants seeking safety and a better life in the US.

Filipino migrant organizations in the United States rallied behind asylum seeker Mark Mabasa, son of slain Filipino journalist Percival “Lapid” Mabasa, after the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) extended his detention for at least another month.

Mabasa was detained in California as his family sought political asylum in the US following the assassination of his father, veteran journalist Percival “Lapid” Mabasa, on October 3, 2022.

His father was the second journalist killed under the Marcos Jr. administration. His killing remains unresolved, with suspect Gerald Bantag, former chief of the Bureau of Corrections, still at large.

The Mabasa family sought asylum in the US after receiving death threats following the journalist’s killing.

On October 2, a day before the fourth year of his father’s killing, overseas Filipino organizations gathered outside Adelanto ICE Processing Center where Mabasa was being detained to demand his immediate release.

The groups were denied entry to the facility, forcing them to hold the protest outside Adelanto City Hall, five minutes awa

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: People-centered energy urged amid ASEAN Energy Forum
content:
Funa-ay Claver, secretary-general of the Kalipunan ng Katutubong Mamamayan ng Pilipinas (Katribu), soeaks during a forum on October 6, 2026. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat

“Energy transition should be an opportunity to develop our self-sufficiency in manufacturing, engineering, and research.”

ASEAN’s energy future is being planned at a forum filled with representatives from corporations, government, banks, and international institutions. Those from grassroots communities are nowhere to be found.

The ASEAN Energy Business Forum was held in Manila from October 5 to 9, bringing more than 1,500 high-level delegates and officials.

“The forum speaks sweetly about innovation, investment, sustainable energy future: identifying projects to fund and profit from,” said Sonny Africa, executive director of think-tank Ibon Foundation, during a parallel conference. “For ordinary people, the essence is not defined by the amount of investments, bankable projects, public-private partnerships, energy companies, and financing but the simplest questions: is the electricity cost lower? Is it more efficient and more accessible?”

The Philippines is assuming the ASEAN chairpersonship this year. Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said that the government will use the opportunity to champion “immediate energy security with long-term resilience.”

author: Aizel Tugalon
title: Progressives renew solidarity with Palestinian resistance
content:
MANILA – Progressive formations led by Philippines-Palestine Friendship Association (PPFA), Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), and International League of Peoples’ Struggle (ILPS) Philippines marched toward the US embassy on the third year since the Al-Aqsa flood. They condemned U.S., Israel and its allies for the continued genocide of Palestine and military aggression on West Asia.

The Al Aqsa Flood refers to the October 7, 2023 attacks led by Hamas that followed Palestine’s long history of resistance against Israel colonial rule and occupation.

For progressives, the Al-Aqsa Flood is not what the west would label as “terrorist attacks” but rather an act of resistance similar to the Philippines, rooted in decades of oppression and colonialism by imperialist nations like the U.S. and Israel. For PPFA, it is the “beacon to our own resistance… It inspires all people struggling for national and social liberation, and therefore, we must support their resistance as if it were our own.”

By the end of the program, progressives burned the flags of U.S. and Israel, calling to stop the genocide, and reaffirming to fight for genuine freedom and the downfall of Imperialism.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Badoy red tags UP Rural High School teacher, community
content:
A teacher and the community of UP Rural High School are the recent targets of red-tagging by former National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC) spokesperson Lorraine Badoy.

On October 6, Badoy red-tagged UP Rural High School teacher Trist’n Buenaflor. Before this, Badoy, in a series of Facebook posts, also red-tagged faculty members and students of the UP Rural High School after the UP Day Remembrance of Martial Law.

The UP Rural High School released a statement on October 1, condemning the red-tagging by Badoy and a military agent named “Emjay Chico.”

“We believe in developing learners who can think critically and engage with the complex problems confronting Philippine society and affecting their basic rights to education, decent life, and human dignity,” the statement reads. “It is deeply concerning that a legitimate educational activity and those who participated in it have been subjected to red-tagging.”

The University asserts the right to academic freedom: fostering discourse that is open, informed, and grounded in evidence.

For his part, Buenaflor has stood his ground.

“All I can say is that I love teaching, and I deeply value my university. I am not afraid,” Buenaflor told Bulatlat in an interview. “I will continue my studies and continue teaching and serving society. I will keep moving forward.”

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Bukidnon Lumad’s fight for ancestral land remains uncertain
content:
Representatives of the Gulinsao and Maranding clans join a dialogue held at Provincial Tulugan Hall, Malaybalay City, Bukidnon, on September 7, 2026. Photo from Bukidnon Provincial IPMR Datu Makayuba Renato Sumbongan’s Facebook page

CAGAYAN DE ORO — After the fifth dialogue aiming to settle the land dispute between Indigenous peoples and a government agency in Barangay Dalwangan, Malaybalay City, Bukidnon, Lumad are still deprived of their ancestral land.

“They should return the land they borrowed,” Datu Aldren Gulinsao told Bulatlat in the vernacular following the dialogue last month.

Since 2017, the Gulinsao clan belonging to the Talaandig tribe has been reclaiming over 600 hectares of ancestral land, while their relative, the Maranding clan, has been claiming over 400 hectares. These form part of the more than 1,000 hectares of land under the title they obtained during the Philippine Commonwealth owned by their ancestor Maximo Gulinsao.

The Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR), on the other hand, said the subject land has been a titled property of the Department of Agriculture (DA) since the 1930s.

To assert their rights, in February, a few members of the Gulinsao clan forcibly entered the land, which resulted in the arrest of three individuals.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Festival-themed protest underscores teachers’ economic demands
content:
MANILA – On World Teachers’ Day, members of the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) held a protest near Malacañang Palace billed as “Pistang Protesta: Dagdag Sweldo, Hindi Dagdag Trabaho.”

Teachers from different public and private schools all over Metro Manila, as well as students and supporters marched Padre Noval Street corner España Boulevard toward Mendiola, October 5, 2026.

Carrying bunting flags and surrounded by ice cream carts, protesters called for a reduced and humane workload, allocation of six percent of GDP to education, P5,000 (approximately US$79.68) economic relief allowance and P50,000 (approximately US$796.81) entry-level salary for all teachers.

The current starting basic pay of a Teacher is pegged at P31,705 (approximately US$505.26) while the economic relief allowance is only P2,000 (approximately US$31.87)

Hogier Villarias, secretary general of Alliance of Concerned Teachers NCR, said that their call for salary hike is timely considering the increase in the country’s Gross Domestic Product.

“Our primary call remains a salary increase since our GDP grew by four percent, so we are expecting that wages should also be increased,” said Villarias, who joined the protest along with his fellow teachers from Andres Bonifacio Elementary School.

author: Josiah David Quising
title: Family, advocates remember 1987 killing of peasant leader, son
content:
Almost four decades later, they still remember. Friends and family held a memorial and candle lighting activity on October 3 to remember Valeriano Caro and his son who were killed 39 years ago by members of the Composite Reaction Force, a unit of the Regional Special Action Force, under the Cory Aquino administration.

Caro was a peasant leader from Kilusang Magbubukid ng Pilipinas (KMP) and chairperson of the Kahublagan sang Mangunguma sa Isla sang Panay (KAMIPA).

He and his son Rolito were killed in Barangay Galang, Oton, Iloilo on October 3, 1987. The memorial and candle-lighting were held on the roadside near the site where they were killed.

According to his wife in a report published by Amnesty International in 1988, Valeriano and her son were taken by the military at around 9:25 a.m. and were shot by a military officer just 70 meters from their own home.

On his 39th death anniversary, Valeriano’s family recalled his dedication to the plight of farmers in Panay.

“His legacy lives on in the continuing struggle to free farmers from landlessness, from bondage to the land, and from abuses at the hands of the regime,” Panay Alliance Karapatan said in a statement. (DAA)

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: ‘Army use of child a violation of int’l humanitarian law’
content:
MANILA – The Philippine Army’s publication of child pictures to pressure a New People’s Army (NPA) member to surrender is a violation of international humanitarian law (IHL), a human rights group said in a statement.

“Posting the child’s name, photograph and location while giving her mother an ultimatum to surrender was not only inhumane and exploitative, it was tantamount to holding the child hostage to compel her mother to do something against her will,” said human rights lawyer Maria Sol Taule, deputy secretary-general of Karapatan, in a statement on October 5.

In a deleted post, the 93rd Infantry Battalion of the Philippine Army published photos of a seven-year-old child with personal details under the pretext of a “birthday party” celebration to urge their NPA mother to surrender.

The Philippines is a signatory to the Geneva Conventions and is obligated to follow the rules of war under IHL. “Children shall be the object of special respect and shall be protected against any form of indecent assault. The Parties to the conflict shall provide them with the care and aid they require, whether because of their age or for any other reason,” the Fourth Geneva Convention stated.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Leyte farmer files harassment complaint vs military
content:
By Veronika Barbosa TACLOBAN CITY – A farmer filed a complaint on September 22 with the Commission on Human Rights Regional Office 8 against the Philippine Army’s 93rd Infantry Battalion (IB) due to intimidation against her and her family.

Accompanied by the National Union of People’s Lawyers Eastern Visayas and Katungod Sinirangan Bisayas, Brenda Lagado said that the first incident happened on July 28 in their house in Jaro, Leyte. “We were visited by elements of the Armed Forces of the Philippines. At first, they were just checking in on us but they eventually pressured us to confess that we have connections with the New People’s Army even if we have none.”

In the same month, Lagado said that her 16-year-old cousin was also interrogated by soldiers and alleged military assets.

“He [my cousin] was tending to farm animal when he was approached by seven soldiers and seven other individuals. At first, he was told to wait for a certain Basas who was supposed to talk to him but the latter did not arrive. He was instead confronted by a certain Simon who later grabbed him by the collar, hit him with a piece of chopped wood, and threatened that he will be hanged or electrocuted if he does not cooperate with them.”

Lagado said that his cousin was coerced by at least 14 men to divulge information about certain individuals that the victim does not know about.

title: Labnotes | Ang kontradiksyon ng renewable energy transition sa Pilipinas
content:
The 54MW Pililla Wind Power Project in Pililla, Rizal is operated by Vena Energy. Photo by Chantal Eco

Sa kalagitnaan ng krisis sa klima, ibinibida ng gobyerno at ng mga malalakihang korporasyon ang transition sa renewable energy bilang solusyon — na ang mga solar, wind farm, at iba pa ay susi sa mura’t malinis na enerhiya. Pero habang kinakalbo ang mga kabundukan para itayo ang wind turbines, solar panels, at mga dambuhalang dams, ang bill ng kuryente—palagi pang tumataas!

Ang mga dapat itanong: sino ang may-ari ng mga planta, sinu-sino ang may kontrol ng transmisyon at distribusyon, at para saan ba talaga ang Electric Power Industry Reform Act o EPIRA?

Patuloy ang pagdami ng mga wind at solar farm sa Pilipinas. Noong 2022, 1,530 megawatt (MW) na kuryente ang mula sa solar, at nadoble ito noong 2025 sa 3,003 MW. Umaabot na ngayon sa 3,892 MW (3.9 GW) ang kapasidad mula sa solar, habang ang wind farm o kuryenteng mula sa hangin ay nananatili sa 427 MW lamang.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: First Person | Losing a home
content:
Screenshot from Baterno's footage.

Losing CMFR feels a lot like losing a home.

I’ve seen many posts about the closure of the Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility (CMFR), and what it means to Philippine journalism.

But to me, it is deeply personal.

Losing CMFR feels a lot like losing a home.

For over 13 years, the center has been the foundation of everything I’ve built in my career. I joined CMFR simply wanting a job experience that would look good on my resume. Never intended to stay because, as a young adult from the Visayas, the goal was to eventually go mainstream.

But a rocky love-hate relationship with my superior during my early years at the organization challenged me to prove my worth as a staff writer. What started as a constant need to prove myself turned into a genuine appreciation for the work and a deeper understanding of why it mattered.

Before I even realized it, I had become deeply involved in its advocacy — tracking threats and attacks against journalists, assessing news reports on various issues, and conducting comprehensive research on media coverage.

CMFR opened doors for me to travel across the Philippines and the world, expand my network, and meet incredible people. But most importantly, it gave me a space to discover stories that I would often draw inspiration from for my own creative side hustles.

author: Aaron Ernest Cruz
title: Seafarers demand end to US war
content:
eafarer groups along with migrant worker groups held a forum to condemn U.S war against countries, affecting their safe travel at sea. (Photo by Aaron Ernest Cruz/Bulatlat)

The Philippines is not just being exploited from their resources but it is also exposed to the enemies of the U.S.

Condrad Belasa, 28, witnessed military aircraft of Iran and the United States carrying out bombings while working as a seafarer. Although their route was far from the Strait of Hormuz, he said that he still felt afraid.

He recalled an incident on March 11, a month after the U.S started its attack on Iran, when their ship passed through the Green Zone. They saw military aircraft bombing one another in real time. Their crew could do nothing but hope that no missiles or ammunition would hit their ship.

“While we are sailing, we see in the radar that we are being followed by military aircraft. Some of my colleagues said it was a fighter jet but in my personal opinion, I think it was a drone,” Belasa told Bulatlat in an interview.

In his five years of working as a seafarer, this was the first time he found himself caught in the middle of a war. The experience worried him, especially because he has a two-year old child waiting for him to come home.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Cultural workers vs fascism, demolition
content:
MANILA — A movement of cultural workers against demolition and police brutality expressed political dissent through a cultural event on September 26 at Vinzon’s Hall, University of the Philippines Diliman.

Dubbed “Gobyerno Sindikato, Panagutin,” Defend the Hood called for an end to fascist measures of the Philippine National Police, including the demolition of their communities.

Skaters, B-boy dancers, graffiti artists, and other performers got together to showcase their talents.

Youth skaters used the occasion to denounce the Marcos Jr. administration’s use of force in repressing and illegally arresting activists, including minors. They also condemned police brutality, citing the violent arrest at the last state of the nation address (SONA) in July where the police illegally arrested 51 protesters.

Among them was Dupa, a member of Defend the Hood and a skater from Pook Malantic in barangay UP Campus.

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: ‘Trump not welcome’
content:
Trump is no ordinary foreign guest.

Should Filipinos welcome guests and express concerns another day?

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro thinks so in relation to the possible visit of United States President Donald Trump to the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit in November.

Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) told Malacañang, “Trump is not welcome in the Philippines.”

“Trump is no ordinary foreign guest,” the group said in a statement. “His waterloo in Iran and West Asia, his continuing support for Israel’s genocide in Palestine, the proxy war in Ukraine, and his unprovoked interventions in Venezuela and Cuba, have made the entire world suffer.”

Castro made the request when asked by a reporter during a Palace press briefing on September 23 if there were additional security measures in place for the 49th ASEAN Summit in Metro Manila, considering what happened to the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC) Investment Forum held at the Grand Hyatt Manila on September 10 where protesters barged to the venue. In this incident, five paralegals who responded to the protest were arrested but were eventually released.

The 1,600-hectare industrial hub under the U.S.-led Pax Silica initiative is planned to be built in New Clark City in Tarlac which is within the LEC.

author: Anne Marxze Umil
title: Not losing hope for 16 years, Mary Jane finally free
content:
Celia Veloso and Mary Jane. (Thomas Andrei Brecio/Pinoy Weekly)

Mary Jane’s release is historical for the overseas Filipino workers.

She was tired as seen in her puffy eyes. But her smile was evident upon being reunited with her loved ones after 16 years.

Finally, Mary Jane Veloso was released from prison.

“I’d like to eat pinakbet and inihaw na bangus,” Veloso replied to a reporter’s question about what she would eat once she is home in Nueva Ecija.

Aside from eating pinakbet, Veloso said that all she wanted was to take a rest.

Veloso was released from the Correctional Institute for Women (CIW) on the night of September 25 after Ferdinand Marcos Jr. granted her absolute pardon.

Veloso spent 16 years in prison, 15 years in Indonesia and a year and half at the CIW.

For Migrante International and National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (among the groups that had led the fight for her freedom), Veloso should have been freed when she came back to the Philippines because she did not commit any crime in the country.

“Kung may tiyaga may nilaga,” Veloso said as she faced the media in a press conference on September 26. She thanked her family who did not leave her in her battle, as well as those who supported her and called on the government to grant her absolute pardon.

title: Faith groups push against US-backed ‘Pax Silica’ hub
content:
Caritas Philippines President Bishop Gerardo Alminaza speaking at the press conference. (Photo by Martha Teodoro/Bulatlat)

Catholic bishops and Protestant leaders, Christian youth and environmental activists are joining forces to halt “Pax Silica,” an AI hub megaproject backed by the United States. Critics fear that this project would drain Central Luzon’s water and power supplies and displace Indigenous communities.

Inked in April 2026, “Pax Silica,” is a U.S.-led worldwide network aimed at protecting supply chains for computer chips, AI tech, and vital minerals. The Bases Conversion and Development Authority has set aside 1,620 hectares in New Clark City in Tarlac for this project, which will be an industrial district for mineral processing sites and automated data centers.

Government officials say the project will turn the Philippines into a worldwide tech powerhouse, but church groups and civil society organizations disagree.

Caritas Philippines President Bishop Gerardo Alminaza called on the national government not to make any binding guarantee all at once.

author: Davao Today
title: Students rally on Martial Law commemoration despite arrest threats
content:
“We should show that we are strong, that we are united here.”

On the 54th year of Martial Law imposition, students joined nationwide protests calling for remembrance, accountability and action.

They took to the streets despite heightened police presence and recent arrests of protesters.

For some students who joined the 54th anniversary commemoration of Martial Law on September 21, the possibility of arrest was not enough to keep them away from the streets. Instead, they said the risks reinforced the importance of being present.

For Alyssa (surname withheld), a Visual Communication student from the University of the Philippines Diliman College of Fine Arts, joining the commemoration was rooted in the right to speak and remember the victims of the dictatorship. “I think the reason why we are here is because even if there are activists being arrested, we should not be afraid to express our call because it is our right to speak.”

She said that the commemoration should not be reduced to a historical date, pointing to the victims of Martial Law and continuing concerns over the treatment of activists.

The National Capital Region Police Office placed Metro Manila on full alert, with more than 15,700 personnel deployed for the September 21 activities. Police said that the deployment was intended to maintain public safety while allowing peaceful assemblies.

author: Jian Sanz
title: University admin cancels human rights docu screening
content:
People at the venue reported the individuals as they were suspiciously taking photos and videos of participants and organizers of the activity from morning to afternoon.

The Isabela State University-Echague administration cancelled the September 21 screening of Noni Abao’s Cinemalaya award-winning documentary, “Bloom Where You Are Planted,” on the eve of the event.

In a statement published on the film’s official Facebook page, the organizers said that despite getting the approval, the administration led by Dr. Artemio Marti Jr. blocked the screening.

School officials claimed that “the activity could be connected to a political gathering of recruiters and anti-government activities in line with the significant date of Martial Law Commemoration,” and warned that a post-screening rally might ensue.

“With this, we see this as a form of censorship of the film,” the Bloom Where You Are Planted team stressed in their post.

Bloom Where You Are Planted depicts the ongoing struggles of human rights defenders and peasant advocates in Cagayan Valley, focusing on the lives of community development worker Agnes Mesina, peasant activist and writer Amanda Echanis, and late peace consultant Randy Malayao.

The College Editors Guild of the Philippines-Cagayan Valley (CEGP) chapter alerted the public on September 20 regarding the presence of suspected intelligence agents at the film’s screen

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: ‘Human rights reparation starts with justice’
content:
Portraits of enforced disappearance victims. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.

MANILA – All human rights violation victims should receive reparation consistent with domestic laws and international obligations.

“From a victim-oriented perspective, the State must recognize that different human rights violations may require various kinds of reparations based on the demands of the victims, their families, and communities which they belong to, to correct the wrongs and achieve healing,” the 2026 Commission on Human Rights (CHR) position paper stated. “Essentially, reparation should be proportional to the gravity of the violations committed and the extent of harm suffered.”

“When my daughter was killed, we received no single assistance nor investigation from the authorities. Not the barangay, not the police. Not one from the government offered help,” Sally Ramos told Bulatlat. Her daughter was killed in 2017 by four unidentified men at the height of the anti-drug campaign.

She said, “We are poor, I do not have a job. My daughter who was killed had a job before she was killed. She supported us for our daily needs and in taking care of my two grandchildren. That is why it was hard for me to accept her passing.”

author: Jian Sanz
title: CLSU Student Regent red-tagged in latest attack on student leaders
content:
Image of packaged sent to Balllesteros (photo from CLSU USSC)

Central Luzon State University Student Regent (CLSU SR) Rashela Ballesteros received a package containing red-tagging messages around 12:30 pm on September 17 at the University Supreme Student Council (USSC) office.

The package, sent by a certain Jared Mariano from Guimba, Nueva Ecija, contained a red-tagging message formatted as a love letter, an altered photo showing Ballesteros’s face pasted onto a soldier’s body, and a list of requirements to become an officer in the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP). The letter in the package read, “Hope I’ll see your smile in campus.(sic)”

In a statement, Anakbayan CLSU condemned yet another harassment and red-tagging of Ballesteros, reiterating that incidents like these result in serious violations of students’ rights to security and freedom of expression.

“This is a threat not only to SR Ballesteros, but also to the democratic rights of the entire CLSU community. It is crucial to protect the freedom of students to voice their demands and participate in social issues, both inside and outside the university,” the youth organization added.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Rights groups assail military-led symposium redtagging progressives in Tacloban university
content:
Photo taken by an attendee during the symposium (name withheld for security reasons).

By Veronika Barbosa TACLOBAN CITY – Progressive groups in Eastern Visayas raised alarm over a red-tagging incident that happened last September 12, 2026 in a symposium led by the 8th Civil Military Operations “Dangpanan (CMO) Battalion inside the Leyte Normal University in Tacloban.

The attendees of the said symposium were students enrolled in the National Service Training Program (NSTP) course mostly composed of first-year students.

According to the accounts of some student attendees, an officer of the Armed Forces of the Philippines discouraged them from joining protest actions. “At first, he [the CMO officer] was only talking about the West Philippine Sea, then we were shocked that they started talking about terror grooming and how it is not necessary to criticize the government through mass mobilizations,” said Aya (name withheld for security reasons), an attendee of the symposium. Aya added that the military officer dissuaded them from joining progressive organizations as it is a form of “terrorist recruitment.” “He said that joining rallies and educational discussions talking about socio-political issues are forms of indoctrination which will eventually lead students to being recruited into the communist rebellion,” Aya told Bulatlat in an interview.

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Impunity persists 54 years after martial law imposition
content:
Symbolic paper cranes were attached in a steel frame, holding the calls for the freedom of all political prisoners. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.

“More than five decades have passed yet the painful legacy of martial law—human rights violations, injustice and lack of accountability—remains deeply entrenched.”

Fifty-four years after the declaration of martial law under the Marcos Sr. dictatorship, political prisoners stressed that abuses continue through corruption and the use of state institutions and laws against dissent.

The warning came from political prisoners detained at the Metro Manila District Jail Annex 4 in Bicutan. They issued a statement through KAPATID ahead of the September 21 commemoration of martial law.

Their statement came days after the Supreme Court overturned former First Lady Imelda Marcos’ 2018 Sandiganbayan conviction on seven counts of graft involving her alleged financial interests in private foundations in Switzerland.

The Supreme Court, in a decision dated June 10 but made public on September 9, acquitted Marcos after finding that prosecutors failed to establish her guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The court cited, among other issues, the failure to properly authenticate key Swiss documents and to establish that the foundations were “businesses” covered by the anti-graft law.

author: Reynard Magtoto
title: Bicol campus journalists, groups unite vs martial law distortion
content:
Standing for the Guild: CEGP Bicol participates in 54th ML protest in Legazpi City to demand press freedom. (Photo by Reynard Magtoto/Bulatlat)

“The martial law continues until now.”

“Martial Law, we will never forget. Defend press freedom.”

Various progressive groups stressed this point at their protest action in Legazpi City, Albay to commemorate the 54th year of Martial Law declaration on September 21.

Bayan Bicol, Condor-Piston Bicol, College Editors Guild of the Philippines (CEGP) Bicol, Kilusang Magbubukid ng Bicol (KMB), BUeños Kontra Korapsyon (BKK), Manibela Albay Chapter and other local groups marched from Bicol University (BU) main campus to Peñaranda Park, calling for accountability from the Marcos Jr. administration and urging Bicolanos to join their efforts against the distortion of martial law history.

“The Marcos family’s campaign of revisionism in Philippine history to erase the bloody and dark history of Martial Law must end,” Bayan Bicol Secretary-General Dan Balucio said. “Marcos Sr. was ousted but still a Marcos is the president today. The martial law continues until now.”

According to CEGP Bicol, the administration has changed but the media workers and campus journalists continue to face the dynastic rule of the Marcoses as they continue to plunder public funds for foreign interests while repressing rights to a free press.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: News in pictures | US-wide campaign against Pax Silica launched
content:
NEW YORK – From the belly of the beast, resistance to the U.S.-initiated Pax Silica is rising.

The U.S.-wide launch of the Shut Down Pax Silica Campaign Network happened on Sunday, September 20 with over 500 people attending in New York City, online, and in watch parties all over the country. Convened by the International League of Peoples’ Struggle-US (ILPS-US), Bagong Alyansang Makabayan USA (BAYAN USA), and International Coalition for Human Rights in the Philippines-US (ICHRP-US), the network consists of 45 organizations who opposed the Pax Silica over impacts on environmental destruction and exploitation of the poor in other countries.

Speakers from Agham, Friends of the Congo, Countermapping Network PH, and Nodutdol shared about the impacts of AI and tech supply chains around the world, and the global threat of Pax Silica, with the Philippines as “ground zero” for the Initiative.

This event marked the beginning of the week of action at the UN General Assembly with the banner “No to War and Plunder, Fight for Peoples’ Rights, National Sovereignty, and Genuine Development.” (RVO)
